newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bombs explode Algiers claim of crushed "terrorism".
newsitem.headline: Bombs explode Algiers claim of crushed "terrorism".

text.p: Bombs in cities and slaughter in villages of Algeria have exploded the government's claim that Moslem fundamentalist "terrorism" has been crushed.

Diplomats and independent analysts in the Algerian capital dismiss Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia's stated belief that political violence is now only "residual" and rebels strike only at lonely, isolated communities.
On the streets of Algiers, the current joke is to refer to Ouyahia as the "residual prime minister".

"It is certainly more than residual terrorism but the government's stability and hold on power are not threatened," said one senior diplomat, referring to two bombs in Algiers on Tuesday that newspapers said killed 20 and wounded at least 111 people.
The bombings came amid a rash of rebel raids on villages in which at least 200 people have died since November. Most choked to death on their own blood after their throats were slit.
"Obsessive fear grips Algeria and surrounding towns", said the newspaper Liberte on Thursday, reporting parents as telling their children to avoid city centres for fear of more bombs.
For many in Algiers, an overcrowded city of about four million people, little has changed since shortly after the time five years ago this Saturday that president Chadli Benjedid was ousted.
He announced live on television that the "dramatic situation" was "a heavy responsibility that I cannot accept". Diplomats said he was ousted in a bloodless coup.

The key element in the "situation" was the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) poised to take power in parliament. It was compounded by catastrophic foreign debt crippling the nation of 29 million people despite its wealth of oil and gas.

The authorities thwarted the FIS by cancelling the election and later banning it. But from its hardline supporters sprang guerrilla groups and about 60,000 people died in the merciless conflict that sucked in thousands of innocent civilians.

"The situation (today) is disastrous. It is not new. The only new element if anything is confirmation the authorities, who believe they can succeed in crushing violence with violence, have failed," said one independent analyst, who asked not to be named.

Economically, ordinary Algerians say little has changed, except for the worse. Pledges of privatisation, so far only a halting process, have brought fear of job losses in overmanned state firms, to add to the 2.3 million officially out of work.
The man in the street shows little faith in Ouyahia's pledge to continue pumping money into state industries to save 400,000 jobs.

Subsidies have vanished or been cut on many basics like bread, tea, semolina, oil, sugar and flour. The government says inflation is down to 16.5 percent against 29 percent in 1995, and forecasts seven percent at end-1997.
"For us, life is harder and more uncertain today than ever," said one middle-aged Algiers resident.
Even the government, in its budget this month, said citizens' purchasing had been cut as it pursues a three-year-old reform policy with the International Monetary Fund.

The relentless pursuit of reform has put Algeria's macroeconomic situation on a much sounder footing. Servicing the foreign debt, which would have taken more than 100 percent of foreign income without rescheduling in 1994, should take 35.5 percent this year, based on a conservative oil price of $17.50 per barrel. More debt rescheduling is excluded.
The $32 billion debt should drop to $26.2 billion in 2000 -- when Algerian officials forecast oil and gas export income should hit $16 billion from the $12 billion expected this year.
Foreign reserves are at a record $4 billion.
But even staunch government supporter Abdelhaq Benhamouda, head of the powerful Algerian UGTA union with more than one million members, says he is fed up.

He plans to set up a new political party. Benhamouda lost his brother in a rebel attack and escaped death himself in another. "Politicians (have) never proposed solutions and alternatives to the social and economic situation," he said last week.

President Liamine Zeroual has promised a general election early this year, followed by local elections. The FIS will be unable to take part. And if the authorities see the polls as a way out of violence, its is not an opinion widely shared.
"The opposing side is carrying violence without a political message any more," said one Algiers-based analyst. "Only violence against violence."
